title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Ecology — 2025
origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-11 ecology unit

questions.question: Define ecology. Name the abiotic factors of a habitat and describe three biotic interactions.
questions.solution:
Ecology is the study of the relationships between organisms and their environment, including other organisms.
Abiotic factors include light, temperature, water, humidity, soil type and pH, oxygen, salinity and wind.
Biotic interactions: mutualism, where both partners gain (alga and fungus in a lichen); parasitism, where one gains and harms the host (Plasmodium in man); competition, where individuals of the same or different species fight for the same limited resource and both lose something.

questions.question: Describe the structural and functional components of a pond ecosystem.
questions.solution:
Structure: abiotic components are water, dissolved oxygen and salts, light and temperature; producers are phytoplankton (algae) plus submerged, floating and marginal plants; consumers are zooplankton and insects (primary), frogs and small fish (secondary) and large fish (tertiary); decomposers are bacteria and fungi in the mud at the bottom.
Function: the four components carry out productivity (photosynthesis by phytoplankton), decomposition of organic debris, energy flow through the grazing food chain and nutrient cycling. Together the four components keep the pond running: energy enters as sunlight, passes through the food web and leaves as heat, while nutrients cycle within the pond. Being small, a pond responds sharply to nutrient input, so nutrient-rich runoff quickly causes blooms and eutrophication.

questions.question: Define food chain, food web and ecological pyramid. State the ten per cent law and give the pyramid of energy in a grassland.
questions.solution:
A food chain is the sequence in which energy passes from producers through consumers (grass → grasshopper → frog → snake). A food web is the network of interconnected food chains in a community. An ecological pyramid is a graphical representation of numbers, biomass or energy at each trophic level.
The ten per cent law says only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next; the rest is lost in respiration, heat, movement and undigested material. So a grassland energy pyramid is always upright, with producers at the base holding the greatest energy.

questions.question: Differentiate gross primary productivity from net primary productivity, and give one reason why a pyramid of numbers can be inverted.
questions.solution:
Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total organic matter fixed by producers by photosynthesis per unit time and area. Net primary productivity (NPP) is GPP minus the energy the producers use in respiration, so NPP = GPP − R; only NPP is available to consumers.
A pyramid of numbers is inverted when one producer supports a great number of consumers, as when thousands of insects feed on a single large tree, or when many small parasites live on one large host. The pyramid of numbers is therefore not a reliable picture of energy flow.

questions.question: Explain the carbon cycle with reference to photosynthesis, respiration and fossil fuels.
questions.solution:
Carbon is fixed as carbon dioxide by photosynthesis into organic compounds and returns to the atmosphere by respiration of plants and animals and by decomposition. Carbon dioxide also dissolves in water and is exchanged between the atmosphere and the oceans.
Some organic carbon is buried and converted into coal, oil and gas over long periods; burning these fossil fuels, along with deforestation and forest fires, releases carbon fixed long ago, so atmospheric CO2 rises faster than photosynthesis can remove it. That imbalance is the main driver of the greenhouse effect and global warming.

questions.question: Describe the nitrogen cycle, mentioning nitrogen fixation, nitrification, assimilation and denitrification.
questions.solution:
Atmospheric nitrogen cannot be used directly by plants. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria — Rhizobium in root nodules and free-living Azotobacter and cyanobacteria — reduce it to ammonia (nitrogen fixation), and lightning and industrial fertiliser manufacture add fixed nitrogen too.
Nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter) oxidise ammonia to nitrite and then nitrate (nitrification); plants absorb nitrate or ammonium and incorporate it into proteins (assimilation). Decomposers release ammonia from dead matter (ammonification), and denitrifying bacteria such as Pseudomonas convert nitrate back to nitrogen gas, closing the cycle.

questions.question: What is ecological succession? Differentiate hydrarch and xerarch succession and define climax community.
questions.solution:
Ecological succession is the orderly, directional replacement of one community by another at a site over time, until a stable community forms.
Hydrarch succession starts in water — pioneer phytoplanktons give way to submerged, then floating and marginal plants, then reeds and finally land vegetation as soil builds up. Xerarch succession starts on bare rock: lichens weather the rock, mosses follow, then grasses, shrubs and trees.
The climax community is the final, self-perpetuating community in equilibrium with the climate of the area, such as a forest in a temperate region.

questions.question: Describe the adaptations of hydrophytes and xerophytes.
questions.solution:
Hydrophytes live in or on water and are adapted to shortage of air and support: a thin cuticle, abundant air chambers (aerenchyma) for buoyancy and gas exchange, poorly developed xylem, stomata on the upper surface only or absent in submerged forms, and long flexible stems.
Xerophytes live in dry habitats and are adapted to conserve water: thick cuticle and waxy surfaces, sunken or hairy stomata, small or reduced leaves turned into spines, deep or widely spreading roots, water-storing succulent tissue and leaf fall in the dry season.

questions.question: Write the causes, effects and control measures of the greenhouse effect and of acid rain.
questions.solution:
Greenhouse effect: CO2, methane, nitrous oxide and CFCs from fossil fuels, deforestation, agriculture and industry trap outgoing infrared radiation, warming the surface. Effects: melting glaciers, rising sea level, floods and droughts, shifting crops and loss of biodiversity. Control: cut fossil-fuel use, plant forests, use renewable energy, improve efficiency and adopt the Paris-type commitments.
Acid rain: sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from burning coal, oil and vehicle fuel dissolve in rain to give sulphuric and nitric acid. Effects: acidified lakes kill fish, aluminium is released, forests are damaged, buildings and monuments corrode and soil nutrients are leached. Control: desulphurise fuels and flue gases, use catalytic converters, switch to cleaner energy and add lime to affected waters.
